**The Last Letter**

I found it in the bottom drawer of my grandmother’s desk, tucked between a yellowed recipe card and a faded photograph of her in a sunhat. The envelope was thin, its edges frayed, and the wax seal had long since melted into a sticky, brown smudge. The address was scrawled in her handwriting, neat but hurried:

*To My Dearest Daughter,*
*No Matter What Happens,*
*Open This When You Need It.*

I hesitated. I didn’t want to know. But curiosity, like a slow leak, had already seeped into my bones.

I tore it open.

The letter was written in her own hand, though the ink had faded to a pale gray. The paper was brittle, the words barely legible in places.

*My love,*
*I don’t know how to tell you this without breaking you. But I have to. You see, I was never your mother. I was your grandmother’s maid. A servant. A girl who came to this house when I was twelve, before your grandmother ever knew me. She took me in, raised me, and when I was sixteen, she married my father. I thought I was her daughter. I thought I was yours. But I was wrong. You were born to her and your father. I was just the woman who cleaned your house, who cooked your meals, who held you when you were sick. I never told you because I loved you. Because I wanted you to think you were special. But you’re not. You’re just the daughter of a woman who never knew she was loved.*

I dropped the letter. My hands shook. The words burned like acid, but I couldn’t stop reading.

*I’m sorry. I wish I could take it back. But I can’t. So I’m leaving. I’m going to start over somewhere else. Somewhere where I won’t have to lie to you anymore. I left you a little money in the safe. Enough to get by. But you’ll have to figure out the rest. I don’t know if I’ll ever see you again. But if you ever need me, I’ll be there. Always.*

I read it again. And again. The truth was a knife in my chest, but it was also a release. No more secrets. No more pretending.

I stood up, my legs wobbly. I had to tell her. I had to tell her everything.

But when I opened the door, the house was empty. The kitchen was cold. The safe was locked.

I sat on the floor, the letter still in my hands. I didn’t know what to do. I didn’t know who to trust.

Then I heard it—a faint, rhythmic tapping. Like someone walking upstairs.

I froze.

The door creaked open. A woman stood there, her face familiar but unfamiliar. She wore a dress I didn’t recognize, her hair tied back in a neat bun. She smiled, but her eyes were hollow.

“You found it,” she said softly.

I nodded.

She stepped closer. “I knew you would. I’ve been waiting for you.”

And then she kissed me.

The letter slipped from my fingers, crumpling to the floor. The house was silent again. The air was thick with something I couldn’t name.

I looked at the woman in front of me. She wasn’t my grandmother. She wasn’t even human.

She was something else.

Something that had been waiting for me all along.

And she was hungry.

(Word count: 1000)
